one_line: Ido Salomon (AgentCraft) argues that humans are the bottleneck in agent work and demos a game-style orchestrator with attention-jumping, a map view, review kits, shared rooms, and a simpler "loopers" mode for non-engineers.
summary: The speaker says agents are capable but supervising many of them at once is exhausting, so the human is the real limit. He presents AgentCraft, a game-inspired orchestrator that wraps Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and similar agents. He builds the talk as a ladder: visibility first (a side panel of agent status and a map that projects the file system and shows which agent touched which file), then autonomy (orchestrators that break a goal into tasks and run them in isolated local containers, plus background loops), then a review kit that shows changes with visual evidence and can compare parallel attempts. Next comes collaboration, with local rooms that others join through a tunnel, shared views of humans and agents, and forking work without being tied to Git. He ends with a lower-floor idea, a simpler mobile-game-style view for people who find the granular tools daunting. The talk is a product demo with a call for feedback, and it contains no measured results.

key_ideas.idea: The human supervisor, not the model, is the bottleneck when many agents run at once.
key_ideas.detail: Steering, reviewing and babysitting each agent is what burns people out at scale, so the goal is to raise the ceiling of what one person can supervise.

key_ideas.idea: Visibility comes first: show each agent's task, last action and current action in one place.
key_ideas.detail: A side panel lets the user see at a glance which agent needs attention. A map view projects the file system and marks which agent is working on which file, with heat maps built from those links.

key_ideas.idea: Borrow RTS-game attention controls: one key jumps to the nearest agent that needs input.
key_ideas.detail: The user can move from one blocked agent to the next to answer questions or approve plans without scanning every session.

key_ideas.idea: Autonomy means giving a broad goal to an orchestrator that splits it into tasks and runs them in isolated local containers, with loops that create work in the background.
key_ideas.detail: Loops can scan sources such as GitHub or social feeds and turn findings into feature work with no upfront prompting. The speaker frames this as the start of software factories.

key_ideas.idea: Reviewing many agent outputs needs a review kit, not a stream of raw diffs.
key_ideas.detail: The kit gathers all changes, offers a per-file view or visual evidence such as videos and screenshots, and can run several instances in parallel so the user picks the best result.

key_ideas.idea: Collaboration means shared rooms that people and agents join, with a common notice board of who is doing what.
key_ideas.detail: Rooms run locally and can be exposed through a tunnel. A designer can produce work that an engineer picks up, forks and continues, so the team is not tied to Git as the only shared workspace.

key_ideas.idea: Lowering the floor matters as much as raising the ceiling: non-engineers have adopted the tool, and a simpler mode is being tested.
key_ideas.detail: Early users include children and people with no coding background. The proposed loopers mode is a simple prompt-result loop with project bookmarks and optional detail. The speaker calls it a very early draft.

techniques.name: Attention queue with jump-to-next
techniques.how: Track each agent's state (running, blocked on a question, waiting for plan approval, done) and bind one key to jump to the most urgent item that needs a human.
techniques.when: Many agents run in parallel and the human cannot watch all of them.

techniques.name: Spatial projection of agent activity
techniques.how: Lay the project file tree out as a map, place markers where each agent touches files or directories, and aggregate the touches into a heat map.
techniques.when: You need to see where agents are working across a large codebase without reading logs.

techniques.name: Review kit for parallel agent output
techniques.how: Collect the full change set per run, provide a per-file view plus visual evidence (screenshots or video), and run N attempts in parallel so the reviewer compares and picks the best.
techniques.when: Several agent runs produce changes that need quick human approval.

techniques.name: Orchestrator with isolated local containers and background loops
techniques.how: Give one high-level goal to an orchestrator that decomposes it into tasks, runs each in its own local container, and schedules loops that scan sources for new work.
techniques.when: Work can run unattended and each task needs isolation from the others.

techniques.name: Shared room with cross-agent notice board
techniques.how: Host a local room, expose it through a tunnel when needed, and show each person and agent's current activity on a shared board so people can fork or hand off each other's work.
techniques.when: A team, including non-engineers such as designers, needs to work on the same agent-driven project.

techniques.name: Progressive disclosure for low-floor use
techniques.how: Default to a simple prompt-then-result view and let users open the file, tool and status detail only when they want it, with customizable layout.
techniques.when: The target users are not developers and the granular views are overwhelming.

numbers.claim: Illustrative only: a user could 'spin up 25 cloud code agents' in the thought experiment.
Anecdotal workload: 'I would say 20, but even five things to review at the same time' is described as hard to manage.
Stated target audience for the lower-floor idea: 'around 90% of the people in the world'. This is a goal, not a measured result.

hot_takes: The human, not the model, is the bottleneck in agentic work.
Real-time strategy and city-builder games are a good model for supervising agent fleets.
Visual evidence (video or screenshots) of agent changes is better for review than reading diffs.
Shared agent workspaces should not be tied to Git as the only collaboration layer.
Agent tooling should be designed for non-engineers too, including children and people with no coding background.

relevance.why: ProsHarness already has phone-driven approvals and checkpointed long runs. The talk's needs-attention queue and review kit for parallel attempts map directly onto those flows.
relevance.action: Add a needs-attention queue to ProsHarness that lists runs blocked on a question or plan approval, ordered by urgency, with a single key to jump to the next one. Feed it from the existing phone-approval events.

relevance.why: AgentOS has L4 observability and agent telemetry. A per-agent activity view could use that data, but the talk shows no measurements.
relevance.action: Prototype a per-agent activity panel on AgentOS telemetry that shows which files or tools each agent touched, using the L4 OTel data.

relevance.why: The parallel-run review kit (diff, per-file view, visual evidence, pick the best) is a reusable pattern for reviewing subagent outputs in any multi-agent setup.
relevance.action: Read the talk's review-kit section and sketch a review bundle for parallel subagent runs: changed-file list, evidence attachments, and a side-by-side pick.
